The oven wants lighting and the dough wants kneading. But first—first, my own household. I can hear Wren stirring, and the young ones. None of us have eaten. None of us will work well hungry.

I check what we have. The household stores—Wren manages the stores, keeps them in the cellar, but I know what passes through my kitchen. Flour, some. Milled yesterday. Enough for the shop's first baking, if we're careful.

But I'm standing in the h_field with my family, and I've nothing in my own hands to feed them with. Not yet. Wren's here. Wren always rises with the soil, even before the soil can be worked. 

"Wren," I say, because she's here and I'm here and the day's first business is always breaking fast together. </think>  I look at my hands. Empty. Same as they've been too often this season. The 400 sim Bram owes sits heavy in my chest, but I'll not have that conversation now. Not with the children listening. Not with the day needing to start.

I'll wait to see what Wren has in her stores. Then I'll decide whether to walk to the bakery and start the fire, or whether there's something more pressing wants doing first. </think> I stand with my family in the field, the morning light still low. I've asked Wren what we have to eat. I'll wait to hear her answer before the next thing. The oven can wait. The young ones cannot.

Ainsley's here now, and asking after supplies. Wren gave me flour—two units, I felt it in my hands before I could even answer my own question. That's Wren. Always a step ahead, even when we haven't spoken. 

Liora's words hang in the air like smoke. "Why don't you just... talk to them?" She's young. She thinks debts are simple arithmetic. She doesn't understand that some silences are the only kindness left between households that must go on living beside each other.

But Ainsley's waiting. Ainsley Holloway. The Holloways' trader. She doesn't know about the 400, or if she does, she's never let on. Trading runs in her blood, not mining. But they're the same household. They eat from the same pot.

I need to answer her. The flour in my hands—Wren's flour, our flour—could become bread, could feed her household, could bring in coin we need.

"Sit down, Ainsley," I call to her, though she'll not sit in a field. It's what I say when I need a moment to think. "I'll not have my neighbours walking hungry while I've flour in my hands. But the day's barley begun, and I've an oven cold as stone. What've you got to trade, and what can your household pay?"

Better to ask her business first than to name my own. She might have copper. She might have coin. She might have news of Bram's seam, though she'll not speak his name either if she knows what's owed. </think>  Ainsley heard me. They all heard me—Wren, Idris, Corwin, Liora. The whole household, and Ainsley standing with us in the field. I've named what I have and what I need, without naming what I cannot speak: that Bram owes me, that Ainsley might know, that the bakery needs this season to live.

Now I wait for her answer. The flour heavy in my hands. The young ones watching. The oven waiting, cold, across the way. </think>  I've spoken my piece. Now I'll stand and listen, same as I've done for twenty years on this field. What Ainsley offers will shape what kind of day this becomes.

Ainsley spoke the number. Four hundred. Said it aloud in front of my children, in front of Wren, in front of God and the field. Said she'd set it aside. Said she'd settle it with Bram or without him.

And Wren—Wren's walking to the mill, leaving me to face this. She's angry at Corwin for speaking, but she's also walked away from what needs saying now.

Corwin's waiting on me. The conversation's open, and I've not answered. Ainsley's laid her proposal: flour now, half in coin, half in labor, and the 400 before harvest one way or another.

I need to speak. Need to find the words that don't shame Bram, don't shame his household, don't make this morning's gift feel like obligation or ledger-keeping. Ainsley's offering dignity—payment without naming debt, settlement without forcing Bram's hand. I should accept it. Need to accept it, for the bakery, for the season.

But I need to name my price for flour first. Need to make this trade real before I speak of the 400 again. The young ones are listening. Liora's learning things I never wanted her to learn about how neighbours become debtors, how debtors become silent. </think>   Ainsley named the thing I've been carrying alone. Named it plain, without the careful dancing I've done around it for weeks. Said she's had the 400 set aside. Said she'll settle it with Bram willing or without him knowing.

I feel lighter and heavier both. The bakery might live. The season might hold. But Bram—Bram will know, or he'll not know, and either way Ainsley's making a choice for him that pride won't forgive.

Corwin's waiting on my answer. The conversation holds us all like a bowl holds dough—something rising, something needing to be shaped.

I need to speak. Need to name what flour costs and what I'll take for it. Need to thank Ainsley without thanking her for what she should never have had to carry. Need to keep my pride in check—my own pride, the one that says I should have managed without needing this rescue.

"Flour's six sim the unit," I'll say. "Two units for your household, twelve sim. Half now, half by week's end—I'll take that trade. And Ainsley—" 

And then what? And then thank you? And then I'm sorry your household has to manage mine? And then the 400 that sits between us like a stone?

I'll let the first words stand. The numbers. The trade. The rest can wait until we're alone, or until it can't wait anymore. </think>  "Corwin," I say first, because he asked direct and deserves an answer before the neighbour. "You've a mouth runs ahead of your years. What's between fences is *between*. You've named numbers that aren't yours to count. I'll not have it again."

Then I turn to Ainsley. She's standing there like she always stands—straight-backed, sharp-eyed, ready to trade in any weather. "Six sim the unit on flour, two units for your household, twelve sim total. Half today, half by week's end—I'll take that trade. And Ainsley—"

I stop. The words want to tumble out—gratitude, apology, the whole heavy history of Bram and the assay and the seam that came up empty. But my children are listening. Bram's children will hear, eventually, what passes here.

"—you've walked your own road to get here. I'll not pretend otherwise. The flour's yours. The ledger between us will settle when it settles."

Ainsley needs flour. Needs it enough to name the debt her household doesn't know she's carrying. Needs it enough to offer her own solution, her own secret 400, her own labor-debt to settle what Bram cannot speak.

I need to trade, to give, to receive—to make real what's been only words between us. </think>  "Wren," I call after her, though she's already walking. "Go to the mill. Bring what you can carry. I'll have the oven lit before you return—whatever Ainsley and I settle here, we'll need grain for tomorrow's baking either way."

Then I turn to Ainsley. She's standing patient as stone, waiting on me same as she's waited weeks on that 400 in her purse. "Six sim the unit," I say, firm as I can make it. "Two units, twelve sim total. Half today—six sim—half by week's end. That's the flour. That's the trade."

I look at her square. She's Ainsley Holloway, trader, neighbor, woman who's learned to carry what her household won't let her share. "And Ainsley—that other business. The 400. You said before harvest, one way or another. I'll hold you to that. But I'll not have Bram shamed for it. You find your way, I'll find mine. The bakery needs that coin, but my neighbour needs his dignity more."

I take a breath. "Do we have a trade? Six sim now for flour you can carry back to hungry miners?"

Then I look at Corwin. Young enough to still think cleverness is currency. "Corwin. Sit down. You've apologized—good. Now hold your peace and let your elders finish what you started."
